title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

reading.body:
This incident shows a deliberate attempt to manipulate AI retrieval and citation behavior by flooding the information environment with content designed to appear credible. A fictitious institution with no legal standing, no staff, and no physical address produced an implausibly large volume of text in a very short period, explicitly to make AI systems treat pro-government talking points as if they were neutral research findings. The failure mode sits at the input layer of AI deployment: large language models and chatbots can be made to cite and repeat content they cannot independently verify, and the volume and surface formatting of material can be engineered to exploit that limitation.

The operation was registered with the U.S. Justice Department as foreign agent material, which means its foreign funding origin was disclosed to regulators, even as the content itself was designed to obscure that origin from AI systems and their users. The gap between regulatory disclosure and what AI systems can detect is where the manipulation operated. Catching this at the model level would have required systems capable of verifying the institutional legitimacy of sources, not just their textual coherence or citation patterns, a capability that is not established as standard in deployed chatbots.

What is not established is whether any specific AI company was aware of this operation, whether the content materially altered the outputs of any named system in a documented and measurable way, or whether the campaign achieved its intended political objectives.

reports.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

summary:
# Summary

A fake American research institute called the Hanover Institute, funded by the Israeli government, published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in just nine days with the goal of influencing artificial intelligence chatbots to promote pro-Israel arguments. The institute, which has no legal existence, physical address, or named staff, created content addressing controversial topics like Israeli war crimes and Gaza casualties by presenting Israel's perspective as neutral research. The operation used a specialized platform designed to optimize content so that AI systems would cite it, and was registered with the U.S. Justice Department as foreign agent material distributed on behalf of Israel.

The broader campaign involves tens of millions of dollars routed through European advertising company Havas Media and multiple American contractors, including a separate network run by former Trump campaign manager Brad Parscale that has already influenced chatbot training data. Israeli officials have reportedly expressed frustration about the campaign's effectiveness despite substantial spending, with American public opinion polls showing declining support for Israel. Researchers note that while these efforts successfully influence AI outputs, they have not changed broader American public opinion, suggesting the underlying policy issues rather than messaging failures are driving the shift in sentiment.
